refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: The accept.d/ directories contain plain ini-style text files that select devices and configure how the kernel may access and operate them. Currently, this is the trust level of a device, which is written to the trust_policy attribute in the sysfs directory of the device. See systemd.syntax7 for a general description of the syntax.

The configuration is applied by systemd-device-accept-d.service8. During boot, it applies the configuration to the devices that exist when it is started, before udev loads the kernel modules for them, and after that to the devices that are added, for example by hotplug. It only applies the configuration when a device is added, since the trust level of a device can only be changed until a driver has been probed for the device. To have the configuration applied in the initrd, the files, as well as the service, have to be included in the initrd. After the files have been changed, use systemctl reload systemd-device-accept-d.service to apply them to the devices that exist.

Note that this cannot change the trust level of devices that have been probed already, for example because their drivers are built into the kernel, or because they were set up before the configuration was available. The trust levels of the devices that built-in drivers might be bound to are passed on the kernel command line when the kernel is installed, see "Built-in Drivers" in systemd-device-accept-d.service8. Failing to apply the trust level to a device is logged. See HoldProbing= in device-accept.conf5 for having drivers bound to the devices on some buses only after the configuration has been applied to them, in which case no driver is bound to a device whose trust level could not be applied, or is disabled.

The files are read from the directories /usr/lib/systemd/accept.d/ and /usr/local/lib/systemd/accept.d/ , the volatile runtime directory /run/systemd/accept.d/, and the local administration directory /etc/systemd/accept.d/. All files are collectively sorted and processed in alphanumeric order, regardless of the directories in which they live. However, files with identical filenames replace each other. Files in /etc/ have the highest priority, files in /run/ take precedence over files with the same name in /usr/lib/. This can be used to override a system-supplied file with a local file if needed. As a special case, an empty file (file size 0) or symlink with the same name pointing to /dev/null disables the configuration file entirely (it is "masked"). Only files with the suffix .conf are read.

Along with the file foo.conf, a "drop-in" directory foo.conf.d/ may exist. All files with the suffix .conf from this directory will be merged in the alphanumeric order and parsed after the main file itself has been parsed. This is useful to alter or add configuration settings, without having to modify the main configuration file. Each drop-in file must have appropriate section headers. Drop-in directories can be placed in any of the directories above. Drop-in files in /etc/ take precedence over those in /run/, which in turn take precedence over those in /usr/lib/. Drop-in files under any of these directories take precedence over the main file wherever located. Note that the accept.d/ directories are not drop-in directories of a main configuration file themselves, but contain the main files, which may have drop-in directories of their own.

Each file contains a [Match] section, which selects the devices the file applies to, and an [Accept] section, which specifies how to configure these devices. The first (in lexicographic order) of the files that selects a given device is applied to it. All later files are ignored for this device, even if they select it as well. Hence, to override the setting of a file for some devices, use a file that sorts before it. No files are installed by default.

Files that do not contain at least one valid selector in their Device= settings, as well as a valid TrustLevel= setting, are ignored, and a warning is logged. Use /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-device-accept-d --dry-run to see which devices the files select, see below.

listitem.para: A whitespace-separated list of selectors, each of which selects devices. A device is selected by a file if it is selected by any of the selectors in any of the Device= settings of it. This option may be specified more than once, in which case the selectors are added to the list. If an empty string is assigned, the list is reset to its initial state, i.e. it is emptied. A selector that is not valid is ignored, and a warning is logged.
A selector has the form type:value. The type is mandatory and case-sensitive, so that a value is never interpreted differently than intended. The following types are supported:

Selects the devices whose kernel name matches the shell-style glob name, in any subsystem. The kernel name of a device is the last component of its sysfs path, such as mlx5_0 or eth0. Note that the kernel name of a PCI device is its PCI address, 0000:01:00.0 for example. Neither the names of devices that are parents of the device, nor alternative names, are considered. Also note that kernel names are not necessarily unique, and that network interfaces may be renamed, see systemd.link5. The name a device has when the configuration is applied to it is used.

Selects the PCI device with the given address, as shown by lspci8, for example pci:0000:01:00.0. The address consists of hexadecimal numbers, of which the case does not matter: the domain, with four to eight digits, the bus, with two digits, the device, with two digits and a value of up to 1f, and the function, with a single digit of up to 7. The domain is optional, and 0000 if left out, i.e. pci:01:00.0 is the same as pci:0000:01:00.0. Only the PCI device itself is selected, but none of the devices that are below it, such as network interfaces or RDMA devices. Globs are not supported.

Selects the devices whose sysfs path matches the shell-style glob path, for example path:/sys/devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:1c.0/0000:05:00.0. The path must be a path below /sys/devices/. The /sys prefix may be left out, as in path:/devices/platform/foo. In globs, wildcards do not match slashes. Only the device with the given path is selected, but none of the devices that are below it. Paths to symlinks of devices, such as the ones in /sys/bus/ and /sys/class/, are not supported, since they are not resolved. Use the canonical path of the device, or pci: for PCI devices, instead.

Since the selectors of a file are alternatives, a file can select any number of devices, of any of the types above, and all of them get the same trust level. To give devices different trust levels, use different files.

The trust level to configure for the devices that are selected by the file, which is written to the trust_policy attribute of the device. The read-only trust attribute reports the active level resolved when a driver binds. The trust level tells how the kernel operates a device. It does not tell anything about the identity of the device, and does not attest its firmware. One of the following values, which are case-sensitive:
Let the bus of the device select the trust level.
Do not allow any driver to bind to the device.
Operate the device as a potentially malicious device, with the restrictions this requires.
Operate the device with the usual privileges.

This setting is required. If an empty string is assigned, the setting is reset to its initial state, i.e. it is not set. If the device already has the trust level, nothing is written. Failing to change it is logged, which is the case if the device does not have the attribute, because the kernel does not support it, or if a matching probe has been attempted already, including a failed or deferred probe. Unbinding does not make the policy writable again. Note that it is up to the kernel to define the exact meaning of the trust levels.

example.title: Operate a PCI network controller as potentially malicious
example.para: Select the controller itself: configuring a network interface does not change the policy of its parent PCI device or the driver bound to that parent.

example.title: Disable the devices below a PCI bridge port, but one
example.para: The wildcard in the second file selects the devices that are directly below the PCI bridge. As the files are processed in alphanumeric order, and the first file that selects a device is applied, the first file here takes the one device it names out of the second one.
